title: Supporting Check: What is the impact on the pairing check if non-subgroup points are accepted?
state_context: Library: github.com/ethereum/c-kzg-4844/v2 v2.1.1. The C library's validate_kzg_g1 function (bytes.c:81-95) calls blst_p1_uncompress (on-curve check) then blst_p1_in_g1 (G1 subgroup membership) for all commitment and proof bytes before any pairing. Called via bytes_to_kzg_commitment (for commitments) and bytes_to_kzg_proof (for proofs) inside verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch. Point at infinity is explicitly permitted.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The Go wrapper layer (kzg.go) performs no subgroup validation, delegating entirely to c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1. The C library's validate_kzg_g1 function calls blst_p1_uncompress (curve check) followed by blst_p1_in_g1 (G1 subgroup membership check) for all commitments and proofs before any pairing operation. The cell_indices parameter receives sidecar.Index (column position 0..127), which is correct for all cells in a DataColumnSidecar. No Go-layer caching of KZG results exists. The kzgVerifierRoutine batches concurrent requests; a single invalid sidecar propagates the error to all co-batched verifiers causing DoS amplification via fallback re-verification.
state_anomalies: Go layer performs zero subgroup validation — all trust placed in C library validate_kzg_g1
One invalid sidecar in verifyKzgBatch sends same error to all co-batched verifiers, causing DoS amplification
Point at infinity permitted as commitment (correct per spec, but represents a special case bypassing the in_g1 check)
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No KZG verification result caching in Go layer. Inclusion proof caching (data_column.go) is separate and does not affect KZG. Each call triggers a fresh C library invocation.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: kzgVerifierRoutine goroutine drains kzgChan and calls verifyKzgBatch. Propagation of a single error to all co-batched verifiers causes forced fallback re-verification. No race condition in verification path itself.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: A crafted Bytes48 containing a G1 curve point outside the G1 subgroup is rejected by blst_p1_in_g1 before any field arithmetic, returning C_KZG_BADARGS which propagates as ErrInvalidKZGProof. No path through verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch reaches the pairing for non-subgroup points. No counterexample for PROP-W5B14-12 was constructed.
attack_scenarios: ATTACK: Send DataColumnSidecar with KzgCommitments[0] set to a valid BLS12-381 G1 curve point not in the G1 subgroup (low-order point). Result: C library returns C_KZG_BADARGS via bytes_to_kzg_commitment -> validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1. ErrInvalidKZGProof is returned. ValidationReject. Bypass FAILS.

ATTACK: Send DataColumnSidecar with KzgProofs[0] set to a G1 point not in the G1 subgroup. Result: bytes_to_kzg_proof -> validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1 returns C_KZG_BADARGS. ErrInvalidKZGProof is returned. ValidationReject. Bypass FAILS.

DoS ATTACK: Continuously send crafted invalid sidecars concurrent with legitimate sidecar gossip to cause batch poisoning, forcing all honest sidecars to re-verify individually. This is resource exhaustion only, not a cryptographic bypass.

phase2_5_reachability.classification: not-exploitable for cryptographic bypass; DoS amplification possible via batch poisoning

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: PROP-W5B14-12 invariant is fully satisfied. The proof path: VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs -> kzg.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch -> ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch -> C verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch -> bytes_to_kzg_commitment / bytes_to_kzg_proof -> validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_uncompress + blst_p1_in_g1. Both commitments and proofs are checked. The check occurs before any pairing computation. Guard is sufficient.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard: validate_kzg_g1 in c-kzg-4844/v2@v2.1.1 bytes.c:81-95: blst_p1_uncompress (on-curve) then blst_p1_in_g1 (G1 subgroup membership). Called for all commitments and all proofs before any pairing.
edge_cases: Point at infinity allowed (blst_p1_is_inf returns OK before subgroup check) — correct per KZG spec for zero polynomials
CELLS_PER_EXT_BLOB (128) == numberOfColumns (128), ensuring C index range check and Go range check are consistent
Go binding checks len(commitmentsBytes) != len(cells) providing defense-in-depth before C call

reasoning: The subgroup check is correctly implemented in the C library (blst_p1_in_g1 in validate_kzg_g1) and is called unconditionally for both commitments and proofs before any pairing. An attacker cannot provide a non-subgroup point that passes the pairing check — the verification returns an error (C_KZG_BADARGS -> ErrInvalidKZGProof -> ValidationReject) before any pairing is computed. The impact of non-subgroup points is correctly handled: they are rejected, not accepted with incorrect pairing results.
recommendation: No fix required for the subgroup validation. The defense is correctly implemented in the C library layer.

title: Supporting Check: Can malicious P2P peer bypass subgroup checks via crafted DataColumnSidecar?
state_context: All validation layers preceding KZG verification: byte length checks (ValidFields), merkle inclusion proof (SidecarInclusionProven), proposer signature (ValidProposerSignature). None of these check subgroup membership — that is handled entirely by the C library. The P2P gossip layer allows any connected peer to send DataColumnSidecar messages. No rate limiting on KZG verification calls.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The complete P2P-to-KZG path is: P2P gossip receive -> decodePubsubMessage -> validateDataColumn -> ValidFields (structural) -> SidecarInclusionProven (merkle) -> ValidProposerSignature -> validateWithKzgBatchVerifier -> kzgVerifierRoutine -> verifyKzgBatch -> VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs -> VerifyCellKZGProofBatch -> C validate_kzg_g1. All 48-byte commitment and proof bytes reach the C library with attacker control. No Go-layer subgroup check exists. The C library's validate_kzg_g1 is the sole subgroup gate.
state_anomalies: No Go-layer subgroup validation — commitments and proofs reach C library as raw bytes
The SidecarInclusionProven check verifies KZG commitments are in the block body via Merkle proof but does NOT check subgroup membership
An attacker who can craft a block with a non-subgroup commitment included in the block body could exercise this path — but the proposer signature check prevents arbitrary block injection
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of subgroup validation results. Each message triggers fresh C library call.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: The kzgVerifierRoutine batches concurrent requests. Batch poisoning is possible (see CHK-0125/batch_verifier.go).

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Full attack scenario trace: Attacker sends DataColumnSidecar over P2P gossip with commitment bytes encoding a G1 curve point not in the G1 subgroup. Sidecar passes ValidFields (structural checks), SidecarInclusionProven (Merkle inclusion of commitment bytes — NOT subgroup check), ValidProposerSignature (verifies block header, not KZG content). Reaches C library. bytes_to_kzg_commitment -> validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1 returns false -> C_KZG_BADARGS. ErrInvalidKZGProof propagates. ValidationReject. Bypass FAILS.
attack_scenarios: FULL ATTACK TRACE: Attacker crafts DataColumnSidecar with commitment=G1_non_subgroup_point. Passes ValidFields (just index/length checks). Passes SidecarInclusionProven (Merkle proof of commitment bytes, not subgroup membership). Passes ValidProposerSignature (block header sig, not KZG content). FAILS at validate_kzg_g1 in C library: blst_p1_in_g1 returns false -> C_KZG_BADARGS -> ErrInvalidKZGProof -> ValidationReject. Bypass confirmed impossible.

ATTACK VECTOR: Can attacker include a non-subgroup commitment in a valid block (signed by the proposer)? YES — the block's KZG commitments are just 48-byte values; the proposer signature covers the block header including BodyRoot which includes the commitment list. But the DataColumnSidecar received at the peer would still fail the C library subgroup check when the peer validates it, preventing the sidecar from being accepted.

CACHED RESULT SUBSTITUTION: Is there a code path where a previously-validated commitment's result is reused without re-validation? No — the KZG verification caches (seenDataColumnCache) cache by (slot, proposer_index, column_index) and gate on the entire validation pipeline passing. No partial cache substitution is possible.

phase2_5_reachability.classification: not-exploitable for cryptographic bypass; subgroup check is the correct first gate for G1 points

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant 'no non-subgroup point passes the pairing check' is proven. validate_kzg_g1 executes before the pairing computation in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch. All commitment bytes go through bytes_to_kzg_commitment -> validate_kzg_g1. All proof bytes go through bytes_to_kzg_proof -> validate_kzg_g1. There is no code path that bypasses these calls. The blst library's blst_p1_in_g1 function is the authoritative subgroup check for BLS12-381 G1 and is known-correct.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard: validate_kzg_g1 with blst_p1_in_g1 in c-kzg-4844 bytes.c — unconditionally called for all 48-byte inputs before pairing
edge_cases: SidecarInclusionProven checks commitment bytes are in the block body via Merkle proof but this does NOT validate subgroup membership — the attacker-controlled commitment bytes can encode any G1 point and still pass the Merkle check
The Merkle check therefore does NOT eliminate the need for the C library subgroup check — the C library check is the essential gate

If an attacker can get a non-subgroup commitment into a valid block (block signed by a compromised proposer), the sidecar with that commitment would still be rejected at the KZG verification step at all peers

reasoning: An attacker cannot bypass the subgroup check via a crafted DataColumnSidecar sent over P2P. The C library's validate_kzg_g1 unconditionally checks blst_p1_in_g1 for all commitment and proof bytes before any pairing computation. All validation layers prior to KZG verification (structural, Merkle inclusion, proposer signature) do not perform subgroup checks, but the C library's check is the correct and sufficient gate. No bypass path exists.
recommendation: No fix required. The defense in depth via the C library's validate_kzg_g1 is correctly positioned and sufficient. Consider documenting that Go-layer code intentionally delegates subgroup validation to the C library as a design decision.

title: Supporting Check: Does verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch assume inputs have passed subgroup validation?
state_context: The Go VerifyCellKZGProofBatch wrapper performs no pre-validation of subgroup membership. It is a thin wrapper around ckzg4844.VerifyCellKZGProofBatch. The C library internally validates all G1 inputs via validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1. The function therefore does NOT assume pre-validated inputs; it validates them internally. This is a key architectural decision: trust boundary at C library boundary, not Go layer.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The Go VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:96-106) performs zero input validation for subgroup membership. It is a raw wrapper: type-casts cells, passes all byte arrays directly to C. This means callers do NOT need to pre-validate. The C function verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch performs its own validation internally. The design is: C library is the trust boundary, not Go. This is a reasonable architectural choice given the C library's specification compliance.
state_anomalies: Go VerifyCellKZGProofBatch has no explicit contract documentation stating whether callers must pre-validate inputs
If a future refactoring adds a new call site that passes pre-validated points through an optimization path bypassing the C library, subgroup checks would be absent
The batch processing behavior (one invalid point causes error for entire batch, not just that point) could be exploited for DoS
phase1_abstract_interpretation.batch_analysis: In batch processing, a single invalid point causes the entire batch to fail with C_KZG_BADARGS. Other points in the batch are not individually reported as valid/invalid. The fallback path in validateWithKzgBatchVerifier handles this by re-validating each sidecar individually.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: The function does NOT assume pre-validated inputs. It validates internally. Call sites traced: (1) VerifyDataColumnsSidecarKZGProofs -> VerifyCellKZGProofBatch: no pre-validation. (2) C library validates all inputs. Mixed batch test: one valid + one non-subgroup point -> C_KZG_BADARGS for entire batch -> fallback -> individual re-verification -> each correctly classified. No implicit trust assumption vulnerability found.
attack_scenarios: ATTACK (mixed batch): Send valid sidecar and invalid (non-subgroup) sidecar in the same batch. C library returns error for entire batch. Fallback validates each individually: valid sidecar passes, invalid sidecar fails. No security bypass.

ATTACK (documentation gap): Future developer adds a call site that passes 'already validated' points to VerifyCellKZGProofBatch expecting no re-validation. The C library still validates internally, so subgroup checks are always performed regardless of caller assumptions. Defense is robust against this.
TRUSTED SETUP G2 POINTS: The G2 trusted setup points (tau*G2, G2) are loaded at library initialization and validated then. They are not user-supplied and cannot be attacker-controlled.

phase2_5_reachability.classification: not-exploitable — C library performs internal subgroup validation regardless of caller assumptions

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: PROP-W5B14-12 invariant is satisfied: VerifyCellKZGProofBatch does NOT assume inputs have passed subgroup validation — it validates them internally via the C library. The invariant 'subgroup check before pairing' is enforced inside the C function, not by callers. This is correct and sufficient. All call sites correctly rely on this internal validation.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard: Internal to C verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch: bytes_to_kzg_commitment and bytes_to_kzg_proof each call validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1
edge_cases: No call site was found that bypasses the C library (e.g., using pre-validated cached G1 points to skip validation). All paths go through the standard C binding.
The trusted setup G2 points are immutable after library initialization and are validated at load time.
Individual vs. batch validation: the C library validates each point within the batch regardless of batch size. A batch of N points results in N individual validate_kzg_g1 calls.

reasoning: The Go VerifyCellKZGProofBatch does not assume callers have pre-validated inputs for subgroup membership. Instead, the C library's verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch internally validates all G1 inputs via validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1 before any pairing computation. No implicit trust assumption vulnerability exists. The architectural choice of placing the trust boundary at the C library level is sound and correctly implemented.
recommendation: Consider adding a code comment to VerifyCellKZGProofBatch (kzg.go:96) explicitly stating that subgroup validation is performed internally by the C library, to prevent future developers from adding intermediate pre-validation or optimization paths that could accidentally bypass this safety gate.

title: Supporting Check: Which cryptographic library implements the BLS12-381 subgroup check, and is it correct?
state_context: Library: github.com/ethereum/c-kzg-4844/v2 v2.1.1 (official Ethereum KZG library, C implementation). Underlying cryptographic primitive library: blst (BLST). The blst_p1_in_g1 function implements the G1 subgroup membership test. The BLS12-381 G1 group has prime order r and cofactor h=76329603384216526031706109802092473003. The subgroup check multiplies the point by r and verifies the result is the point at infinity. The BLST library is a widely-audited, production-grade cryptographic library used throughout the Ethereum ecosystem.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The cryptographic library implementing the subgroup check is c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 (Go bindings) using blst for the underlying G1 operations. The subgroup check implementation: validate_kzg_g1 in bytes.c calls blst_p1_uncompress (on-curve check via decompression) then blst_p1_in_g1 (G1 subgroup membership). The blst_p1_in_g1 function is called via the C FFI from Go. Library version 2.1.1 was released 2024-2025 and includes EIP-7594 (PeerDAS) support.
state_anomalies: No version pinning verification in code — the go.sum file should be checked to ensure the library is not tampered with (standard Go module security)
The Go binding uses CGo which introduces interface complexity; any memory safety issue in the CGo boundary could potentially affect subgroup check results

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Library correctness analysis: (1) blst_p1_in_g1 correctness: The blst library implements the fast G1 subgroup check using the Bowe endomorphism method, which avoids the expensive scalar multiplication by r. This method is mathematically equivalent and has been verified in multiple academic works. (2) validate_kzg_g1 correctness: Calls blst_p1_uncompress (rejects invalid curve points at deserialization), then blst_p1_in_g1 (rejects off-subgroup points). (3) Call sites: bytes_to_kzg_commitment and bytes_to_kzg_proof both call validate_kzg_g1. No code path exists that deserializes G1 points without calling validate_kzg_g1. (4) Known CVEs: No known CVEs for blst_p1_in_g1 or c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 in the public NVD database as of audit date.
attack_scenarios: KNOWN CVE CHECK: c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 released 2024/2025 — no known public CVEs affecting subgroup checks. The blst library has been formally audited by multiple security firms.

DESERIALIZATION BYPASS: Is there an 'unsafe' deserialization function in the Go bindings that skips validate_kzg_g1? No — the ckzg4844.Bytes48 type is passed directly to C and always goes through bytes_to_kzg_commitment or bytes_to_kzg_proof.

CGo BOUNDARY: Memory corruption at the CGo boundary could theoretically affect the subgroup check return value. However, this would require a memory safety bug in the C library itself, not a logical vulnerability in the check.

entry_points: All KZG verification paths — both P2P gossip and RPC sync
phase2_5_reachability.classification: not-exploitable — no known vulnerability in the subgroup check implementation or the library version used

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The subgroup check is implemented correctly in c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 using blst. The validate_kzg_g1 function correctly performs both curve-membership (decompression) and G1 subgroup membership (blst_p1_in_g1). The library is the authoritative implementation for Ethereum KZG operations and is used by all major Ethereum clients. No bypass of the subgroup check was identified. The library version (v2.1.1) is current and includes EIP-7594 support.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard: blst_p1_in_g1 in blst library, called via validate_kzg_g1 in c-kzg-4844 bytes.c, for all G1 point deserialization
edge_cases: The blst library uses the Bowe endomorphism fast subgroup check (not scalar multiplication by r) — this is mathematically proven equivalent and is the standard approach used in production
The point at infinity passes validate_kzg_g1 (checked before blst_p1_in_g1) — this is correct per spec and standard for KZG
go.sum file verifies module hashes — standard Go security tooling prevents dependency substitution attacks

reasoning: The subgroup check is implemented in the well-audited c-kzg-4844 v2.1.1 library using the blst cryptographic library. The implementation (validate_kzg_g1 -> blst_p1_in_g1) is mathematically correct, using the Bowe endomorphism fast subgroup check. No known CVEs affect this version. The check is called unconditionally for all G1 inputs (both commitments and proofs) before any pairing. No bypass exists at the library implementation level.
recommendation: No fix required. The library implementation is correct. Ensure go.sum is committed and verified in CI to prevent dependency tampering. Monitor c-kzg-4844 and blst security advisories for future vulnerabilities.

title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity for tb-002: Does commitment deduplication in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch preserve semantic equivalence?
state_context: The deduplicate_commitments function in the C library (eip7594.c) builds commitment_indices by byte-equality comparison of 48-byte commitment values. The commitment_indices array is entirely independent of the cell_indices array (which contains column positions). Weight accumulation in compute_weighted_sum_of_commitments uses commitment_indices[i] to bind each cell's random weight to the correct unique commitment. The cell_indices (sidecar.Index, column positions 0..127) are used separately for coset factor computation in the polynomial evaluation.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The commitment deduplication in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch operates on byte-equality of the 48-byte commitment values. The 'commitment_indices' produced by deduplicate_commitments are indices into a deduplicated unique commitment list. These are SEPARATE from the 'cell_indices' (column positions, 0..127) passed as the sidecar.Index values. The weight accumulation correctly uses commitment_indices, not cell_indices, to bind weights to commitments. The Go layer correctly passes: (a) per-blob commitment bytes as commitments[], (b) sidecar.Index (column position) as indices[], (c) per-blob cell data as cells[], (d) per-blob KZG proofs as proofs[]. This is semantically correct for the DataColumnSidecar structure: all blobs in a column are at the same column position.
state_anomalies: All blobs within a single DataColumnSidecar share the same sidecar.Index as their cell_index — this is correct semantically but unusual (N cells all with the same column index)

When multiple sidecars from different columns are batch-verified in verifyKzgBatch, cell_indices will contain different values (e.g., [0,0,0,42,42,42,127,127,127] for three sidecars with 3 blobs each at columns 0, 42, 127) — this is correct

The commitment deduplication by byte-equality means two blobs with the same content (and thus same commitment) in different columns would be deduplicated — the math still works correctly since all their cells at their respective column positions would be grouped under the same commitment weight

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: Detailed trace of commitment_indices construction for an adversarial case: Suppose sidecars for columns 0 and 1, each with 2 blobs, with commitments C_A, C_B for column 0 and C_B, C_C for column 1 (C_B appears in both). Go constructs: commitments=[C_A, C_B, C_B, C_C], indices=[0,0,1,1], cells=[cell_0_0, cell_0_1, cell_1_0, cell_1_1], proofs=[P_0_0, P_0_1, P_1_0, P_1_1]. C library: deduplicate_commitments finds unique=[C_A, C_B, C_C], commitment_indices=[0,1,1,2]. Weight accumulation: C_A gets r^0, C_B gets r^1+r^2, C_C gets r^3. The aggregated commitment = r^0*C_A + (r^1+r^2)*C_B + r^3*C_C. This is mathematically correct for the batch verification equation. The cell positions (indices=[0,0,1,1]) correctly specify which coset each cell belongs to for polynomial evaluation. No misalignment found.
attack_scenarios: ATTACK (off-by-one): Suppose commitment_indices computed by deduplicate_commitments has an off-by-one. Analysis: deduplicate_commitments iterates over the input commitments array and assigns each commitment the index of its first occurrence in the unique list. This is a straightforward O(n^2) deduplication. Off-by-one requires the index to start at 1 instead of 0, or to use 1-based indexing incorrectly. The C library uses 0-based indexing throughout. No off-by-one was found in the algorithm description.

ATTACK (attacker crafts same commitment for two different blobs): C_commit_0 == C_commit_1 (byte-equal). Deduplication merges them. commitment_indices = [0, 0]. Weight = r^0 + r^1 for one commitment. But the two cells contain different data (different blobs at different column positions). The pairing equation would be: e(r^0*cell_0 + r^1*cell_1 aggregated, G2) == e((r^0+r^1)*C, tau*G2 - x*G2). If the commitment C truly commits to both cells correctly (which it can only if both blobs are identical), this passes. If the blobs are different but the attacker crafted identical commitments for them (which would mean the commitment is invalid for at least one blob), the verification fails because the pairing would not balance. The cryptographic binding of the commitment to the polynomial prevents forgery here.

ATTACK (correct deduplication but wrong weight accumulation): Is there a case where commitment_indices[i] is correct but r_powers[i] is wrong? r_powers are computed as consecutive powers of r (the Fiat-Shamir challenge). They are independent of commitment_indices. The weight accumulation correctly multiplies r_powers[i] * cell_data[i] and commitment_weights[commitment_indices[i]] += r_powers[i]. No misalignment between powers and indices found.

phase2_5_reachability.classification: not-exploitable for commitment index misalignment; deduplicate_commitments correctly maps by byte-equality and is independent of cell_indices

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: INV-003 invariant: 'For all k, deduplicated_commitments[commitment_indices[k]] == original_commitment_bytes[k].' This invariant is satisfied by deduplicate_commitments which builds the unique commitment list and commitment_indices by byte-equality scan. The weight accumulation correctly uses commitment_indices to bind weights to unique commitments. The Go layer correctly passes commitment bytes (per-blob, from sidecar.KzgCommitments[i]) and column positions (sidecar.Index) as separate semantic entities that map to the correct C library parameters.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard: deduplicate_commitments in c-kzg-4844 eip7594.c — byte-equality comparison to build unique commitment list and commitment_indices array, independent of cell_indices
edge_cases: All-unique commitments: commitment_indices = [0,1,2,...,n-1], weights are all distinct r^i. Correct.
All-identical commitments: commitment_indices = [0,0,...,0], total weight = r^0+r^1+...+r^{n-1}. Correct — only one unique commitment accumulates all weights.
Alternating duplicates: C_A, C_B, C_A, C_B: unique = [C_A, C_B], commitment_indices = [0,1,0,1]. Weights: C_A gets r^0+r^2, C_B gets r^1+r^3. Correct.

BATCH POISONING (informational): verifyKzgBatch in batch_verifier.go:194-214 sends the SAME verificationErr to all co-batched kzgVerifiers when any one fails. This causes all honest co-batched sidecars to fall back to individual re-verification (validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg). The fallback correctly classifies each sidecar. DoS amplification: O(1) attacker work causes O(n) extra verification work where n is the batch size. Not a commitment-index correctness issue, but a resource management concern.

reasoning: The commitment deduplication in verify_cell_kzg_proof_batch correctly preserves semantic equivalence. The deduplicate_commitments function builds commitment_indices by byte-equality (independent of cell_indices/column positions), and weight accumulation uses commitment_indices to correctly bind weights to unique commitments. The Go layer correctly constructs the per-blob commitment array and uses sidecar.Index (column position) as cell_indices, which is semantically correct. No off-by-one or index misalignment vulnerability was found. However, there is an informational-severity batch poisoning DoS: a single invalid sidecar in verifyKzgBatch causes the same error to be sent to all co-batched verifiers, forcing double-verification of all honest co-batched sidecars.
recommendation: For the informational batch poisoning DoS: In verifyKzgBatch (batch_verifier.go:194-214), instead of propagating the same error to all co-batched verifiers when the batch fails, consider re-verifying each verifier's sidecars individually and sending individualized results. This would prevent an attacker from doubling the verification cost of honest sidecars. Current code: 'for _, verifier := range kzgBatch { verifier.resChan <- verificationErr }'. Improved: fall back to individual verification per verifier in the batch when the batch fails, avoiding the shared-error propagation. Note: the current validateWithKzgBatchVerifier already handles this by calling validateUnbatchedColumnsKzg as a fallback for the requesting goroutine — the fix would be to do this per-verifier in the batch routine rather than sending the same error to all.
